title: Neuron
summary: A nerve cell that sends electrical and chemical signals.

layers.basics: Neurons collect signals with branches (dendrites), decide whether to fire, and send pulses along a long fiber (axon).
layers.deeper: The soma holds the nucleus; the axon may be wrapped in insulating myelin; synapses at the tips release neurotransmitters.
layers.expert: Resting potential ≈ -70 mV; action potential via voltage-gated Na+/K+ channels; axon lengths up to ≈ 1 m; ≈ 10^3-10^4 synapses per cortical neuron.

did_you_know: Some neurons in your leg are about a meter long, the longest cells in the body.

title: Astrocyte
summary: A star-shaped glial cell that supports neurons.

layers.basics: Astrocytes feed neurons, tidy up chemicals, and help form the blood-brain barrier.
layers.deeper: They wrap synapses and regulate extracellular K+ and glutamate.
layers.expert: Express GFAP, AQP4 at endfeet; take up glutamate via EAAT1/2; AQP4 at endfeet is implicated in the debated glymphatic clearance model. One of several glial types: all glia together are roughly as many as neurons in the human brain (ratio at or below about 1:1), and astrocytes are only a fraction of them.

facts: ≈ 10× more in human cortex than in rodent
did_you_know: Astrocytes in human cortex are about 2.6 times wider than those of mice and rats, and they extend about ten times more main branches.
open_questions: Does the glymphatic system move fluid by bulk flow, and what role does AQP4 at astrocyte endfeet play?
How much do astrocytes actively shape synaptic signalling?

title: Red blood cell (erythrocyte)
summary: A disc-shaped cell packed with hemoglobin to carry oxygen.

layers.basics: Red blood cells carry oxygen from lungs to tissues. They have no nucleus, so there's more room for hemoglobin.
layers.deeper: Their biconcave shape gives a large surface and flexibility to squeeze through capillaries. They live ≈ 120 days.
layers.expert: ≈ 270 million hemoglobin molecules per cell; glycolysis only (no mitochondria); spectrin-actin skeleton; removed by splenic macrophages; ≈ 2×10^6 made per second.

did_you_know: Each second your marrow releases about two million new red blood cells.

title: Neutrophil
summary: The most common white blood cell and a first responder to bacteria.

layers.basics: Neutrophils race to infections and engulf germs.
layers.deeper: They live only hours to days; measurements of how long vary a lot. Pus is a mix of dead neutrophils, microbes, debris and fluid.
layers.expert: Multilobed nucleus; granules with myeloperoxidase; NETosis; chemotaxis toward IL-8 and fMLP; ≈ 50-70% of leukocytes.

did_you_know: You make about 100 billion neutrophils each day.
open_questions: How long do human neutrophils actually live in blood and in tissue?

title: Macrophage
summary: A large cell that swallows microbes and debris and alerts other immune cells.

layers.basics: Macrophages are the clean-up crew and sentries of the immune system.
layers.deeper: They engulf (phagocytose) germs and display fragments to T cells.
layers.expert: Differentiate from monocytes or arise from embryonic precursors (tissue-resident); polarization states (M1/M2 simplification); express TLRs and scavenger receptors.

did_you_know: Specialized macrophages exist in many organs: Kupffer cells in the liver, microglia in the brain.

title: T lymphocyte (T cell)
summary: A white cell that coordinates or carries out targeted attacks.

layers.basics: T cells recognize specific invaders, and some kill infected cells directly.
layers.deeper: They mature in the thymus. Helper T cells coordinate; cytotoxic T cells kill; memory T cells remember.
layers.expert: TCR recognizes peptide-MHC; CD4+ helper vs CD8+ cytotoxic; costimulation via CD28; regulatory T cells maintain tolerance; rearrangement could in principle make far more receptor types than a person carries at one time.

facts: far more possible than any person carries at once
did_you_know: The number of receptors that rearrangement could in principle produce is far larger than the number of T cells you carry, so most receptor types are present in only a few copies.

title: B lymphocyte (B cell)
summary: A white cell that becomes an antibody-producing factory.

layers.basics: When a B cell recognizes a germ, it multiplies and its descendants release antibodies.
layers.deeper: Memory B cells make later responses faster and stronger.
layers.expert: BCR diversity from V(D)J recombination; somatic hypermutation and class switching in germinal centers; plasma cells secrete antibodies at a very high rate that varies widely between cells and methods.

did_you_know: A single plasma cell is one of the most prolific protein-secreting cells in the body.

title: Platelet (thrombocyte)
summary: A cell fragment that plugs breaks in blood vessels.

layers.basics: Platelets stick to wounds and to each other to form a plug and start a clot.
layers.deeper: They are pieces of giant marrow cells (megakaryocytes) and last about a week.
layers.expert: Activated via collagen/GPVI and thrombin; α- and dense granules; integrin αIIbβ3 binds fibrinogen; ≈ 150-400×10^9/L.

did_you_know: Platelets have no nucleus, they are fragments of larger cells.

title: Cardiomyocyte (heart muscle cell)
summary: The striated, branching muscle cell of the heart.

layers.basics: Heart cells contract in unison to pump blood.
layers.deeper: They are rich in mitochondria and linked end to end by intercalated discs.
layers.expert: Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release via L-type channels and ryanodine receptors; T-tubules; one or two nuclei; limited renewal: carbon-14 dating gave ≈ 1%/yr at age 25, falling to ≈ 0.45%/yr at 75 (Bergmann 2009), though other studies differ.

did_you_know: Carbon-14 dating suggests fewer than half of your heart muscle cells are replaced during a normal life, so most are as old as you are.
open_questions: How much do adult human cardiomyocytes renew, and can this be boosted after a heart attack?

title: Skeletal muscle fiber
summary: A long multi-nucleated cell packed with contractile units.

layers.basics: A muscle fiber is a single giant cell that shortens when stimulated.
layers.deeper: Formed by fusion of many precursor cells, it has hundreds of nuclei lined along the edge.
layers.expert: Contains myofibrils of repeating sarcomeres; T-tubule/SR triads; fiber types I, IIa, IIx; satellite cells enable regeneration.

facts: up to many centimetres in the longest muscles
did_you_know: A single muscle fiber is a giant cell that can be many centimetres long, though in long muscles it is often shorter than the muscle itself.

title: Smooth muscle cell
summary: A spindle-shaped cell that contracts slowly and steadily.

layers.basics: These cells squeeze vessels and organs without conscious control.
layers.deeper: They are not striped and use actin and myosin arranged more loosely.
layers.expert: Ca2+-calmodulin MLCK phosphorylates myosin light chain; caveolae; dense bodies anchor filaments; capable of proliferation and phenotypic switching.

did_you_know: They can maintain tension for hours at very low energy cost.

title: Hepatocyte (liver cell)
summary: The main liver cell, a versatile chemical worker.

layers.basics: Hepatocytes process nutrients, make proteins and bile, and neutralize toxins.
layers.deeper: They are the main cell type of the liver and have lots of mitochondria and smooth ER.
layers.expert: Express CYP450 enzymes, albumin, clotting factors; glycogen storage; polyploid (often tetraploid); can re-enter the cell cycle after injury.

did_you_know: Radiocarbon dating shows human liver cells are replaced continuously, so the average age of liver cells is under 3 years. Liver cells with extra chromosome sets divide much less often than ordinary ones.

title: Enterocyte (intestinal absorptive cell)
summary: A tall absorbing cell lining the intestine.

layers.basics: Enterocytes pick up nutrients from digested food.
layers.deeper: Their top surface bristles with microvilli, forming the brush border.
layers.expert: Express SGLT1, GLUT5, peptide transporters; tight junctions; renewed every ≈ 3-5 days from crypt stem cells.

did_you_know: The surface of each absorptive cell carries a great many microvilli; together with villi and folds this multiplies the gut's absorptive area many times over.

title: Osteocyte
summary: A mature bone cell living inside the bone it built.

layers.basics: Osteocytes are trapped in tiny pockets inside bone and are thought to sense mechanical load, although exactly how is still debated.
layers.deeper: They talk to each other through thin channels.
layers.expert: Dendritic network in canaliculi; secrete sclerostin and FGF23; ≈ 90-95% of bone cells; lifespan of decades.

did_you_know: Osteocytes are the longest-lived bone cells, living for decades.
open_questions: How do osteocytes detect load: fluid flow in their channels, strain in the matrix, or both?

title: Osteoblast
summary: A cell that builds new bone.

layers.basics: Osteoblasts lay down the collagen frame of bone and then mineralize it.
layers.deeper: They come from stem cells in marrow and periosteum.
layers.expert: Secrete osteoid (type I collagen), alkaline phosphatase; signal to osteoclasts through RANKL/OPG; some become osteocytes.

did_you_know: Many osteoblasts end up buried in the bone they make and become osteocytes.

title: Osteoclast
summary: A large cell that dissolves old bone.

layers.basics: Osteoclasts break down bone so it can be renewed and calcium released.
layers.deeper: They form from fused blood-cell precursors.
layers.expert: Multinucleated; ruffled border; secrete H+ and cathepsin K; RANKL-dependent differentiation.

did_you_know: In adults the skeleton as a whole is remodelled over roughly ten years, with spongy bone renewed faster than dense bone.

title: Chondrocyte
summary: The cartilage cell, living in tiny cavities of its own matrix.

layers.basics: Chondrocytes make and maintain cartilage.
layers.deeper: They live in lacunae and get nutrients by diffusion because cartilage has no vessels.
layers.expert: Produce collagen II and aggrecan; hypoxic metabolism; hypertrophy in growth plates leading to ossification.

did_you_know: Cartilage heals poorly partly because chondrocytes are few and isolated.

title: Keratinocyte
summary: The main skin cell, which fills with tough keratin protein.

layers.basics: Keratinocytes are made deep in the epidermis, rise to the surface, flatten and die as a waterproof shield.
layers.deeper: They take about 4 weeks or more to travel from bottom to top, depending on age and body site.
layers.expert: Differentiation: basal (K5/K14) to spinous (K1/K10) to granular (filaggrin, loricrin) to cornified envelope; desmosomal adhesion.

facts: about 4 weeks or more (varies with age and site)
did_you_know: Your outermost skin cells are dead keratin-filled flakes.

title: Adipocyte (fat cell)
summary: A cell storing energy as a large fat droplet.

layers.basics: Fat cells are mostly one huge oil droplet that pushes everything else to the edge.
layers.deeper: They also release hormones like leptin.
layers.expert: Unilocular lipid droplet ≈ 90% of volume; lipolysis via HSL/ATGL; number set largely by adolescence, with ≈ 10%/yr turnover.

did_you_know: The number of fat cells is largely fixed by adulthood; cells change size more than number.

title: Fibroblast
summary: The cell that builds the connective-tissue fibers.

layers.basics: Fibroblasts make collagen and repair wounds.
layers.deeper: When a wound forms they divide, migrate in, lay down collagen and pull the edges together; the repaired tissue is denser and less organized than the original.
layers.expert: Activated to myofibroblasts in wound healing; collagen I/III synthesis; ECM remodeling by MMPs.

did_you_know: Scars are essentially dense collagen made by fibroblasts.

title: Rod photoreceptor
summary: A retinal cell specialized for dim light.

layers.basics: Rods let you see at night, but only in shades of gray.
layers.deeper: They contain a light-catching pigment (rhodopsin) stacked in discs.
layers.expert: ≈ 9.2×10^7 per eye (78–107 million; Curcio et al. 1990); single-photon sensitivity; rhodopsin with 11-cis-retinal; phototransduction via transducin-PDE6 cascade; hyperpolarizes in light.

did_you_know: A dark-adapted rod can respond to a single photon.

title: Cone photoreceptor
summary: A retinal cell for color and sharp daylight vision.

layers.basics: Cones detect color and fine detail in bright light.
layers.deeper: Three kinds respond best to short (blue-violet), medium (green) and long (yellow-green) wavelengths; the long kind is often called "red", which is a simplification. The brain compares the three signals to see all colours, including red.
layers.expert: ≈ 4.6×10^6 per eye (4.1–5.3 million; Curcio et al. 1990), concentrated at the fovea; S, M, L opsins; faster, less sensitive than rods.

did_you_know: Many people with color-vision deficiency lack one of the three cone pigments or have a shifted one.

title: Sperm cell
summary: The male gamete, a tiny swimming cell carrying half a set of chromosomes.

layers.basics: A sperm swims with a whip-like tail to reach an egg.
layers.deeper: It carries 23 chromosomes, an acrosome of enzymes for entering the egg, and mitochondria in the midpiece to power its tail.
layers.expert: Head with nucleus and acrosome, midpiece packed with mitochondria, flagellum; ≈ 45-60 µm long; typical semen holds tens of millions per mL; WHO reference limits are 5th centiles of fertile men, not an infertility cutoff.

did_you_know: Sperm cells are among the smallest human cells but must travel a long way relative to their size.

title: Egg cell (oocyte)
summary: The female gamete, the largest human cell.

layers.basics: The egg carries half the genetic instructions and nutrients that start a new person.
layers.deeper: It is surrounded by a protective coat and cells.
layers.expert: Arrested in prophase I from before birth (for years to decades) until the LH surge just before ovulation, then arrested in metaphase II until fertilization; zona pellucida; ≈ 120 µm.

facts: 23 at ovulation (each still two chromatids); meiosis II finishes only at fertilization
did_you_know: It is just visible to the naked eye.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell
summary: A cell that can renew itself and produce all blood cell types.

layers.basics: Stem cells in your marrow are the source of every blood cell.
layers.deeper: They spend most of their time dormant. A leading idea is that rare division limits copying errors and damage, but that is a hypothesis.
layers.expert: Defined by function (long-term self-renewal and engraftment), not by markers; CD34+ CD38- enriches them but most such cells are not long-term stem cells; niches in marrow; transplant therapy; clonal hematopoiesis rises with age.

did_you_know: One estimate puts the stem cells actively making your white blood cells at about 50,000 to 200,000.
open_questions: How do stem-cell niches regulate self-renewal versus differentiation in aging?
How many stem cells actively contribute to human blood at any time, and how often does each divide?

title: Melanocyte
summary: A skin cell making the pigment melanin.

layers.basics: Melanocytes shade your skin against UV light.
layers.deeper: They pass pigment packages to neighbouring cells.
layers.expert: Melanosomes with eumelanin/pheomelanin transferred to ≈ 36 keratinocytes each; density roughly similar across skin tones.

did_you_know: People of all skin tones have roughly the same number of melanocytes; they differ in how much pigment is made.

title: Pancreatic beta cell
summary: The insulin-secreting cell of the pancreas.

layers.basics: Beta cells sense blood sugar and release insulin.
layers.deeper: They store insulin in granules ready to release.
layers.expert: Glucose enters through GLUT transporters (GLUT2 in rodents; mainly GLUT1/GLUT3 in humans) and is phosphorylated by glucokinase, ATP-sensitive K+ channels close, depolarization, Ca2+ influx, insulin exocytosis (biphasic).

did_you_know: Beta cells sit in islets and work like glucose sensors.
